triage.name: Flu
triage.reason: Common acute febrile respiratory illness with clear presentation and important complications and mimics; well suited to interview and exam-based diagnosis.

demographics: Occurs in all ages; school-age children and their household contacts are most often affected during seasonal outbreaks
Adults 65 and older, children under 5, and pregnant people account for most severe cases and hospitalizations

risk_factors.text: Close contact with someone who has influenza (household, school, workplace, crowded settings)
Not vaccinated against influenza this season
Chronic lung, heart, kidney, liver, blood, or metabolic disease
Residence in a long-term care facility
Occupational exposure such as health care work

comorbidities: Congestive heart failure or coronary artery disease
social_history: School, daycare, or workplace exposure during flu season
Crowded living conditions or group housing
Recent travel or attendance at large gatherings
exposures: Sick contacts with fever, cough, and body aches
Influenza circulating in the community during fall or winter months
Touching contaminated surfaces then the face

chief_complaints.text: I feel like I got hit by a truck
I suddenly got a fever and chills
I have a cough and my throat hurts
I'm so tired I can't get out of bed

hpi.onset: Sudden, over a few hours; patients often can name the hour they started feeling sick
hpi.duration: Symptoms peak in 1–2 days and usually improve over 3–7 days, though cough and fatigue can linger for 1–2 weeks
hpi.progression: Abrupt onset of fever, chills, and body aches, followed by sore throat, nasal congestion, and cough; symptoms are worst in the first 2–3 days then gradually ease
hpi.location: Generalized; centered on the head, throat, and chest
hpi.radiation: Body aches are diffuse and not localized
hpi.quality: Dry or minimally productive cough, scratchy sore throat, deep muscle aching, and a heavy, washed-out fatigue
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; patients often describe it as the worst they have felt in years
hpi.timing: Continuous through the day; fever tends to be highest in the evening and night
pertinent_negatives: Gradual onset over several days (more typical of a common cold)
Predominantly nasal congestion and sneezing with mild symptoms and no fever
Productive cough with colored sputum for weeks
Sudden one-sided chest pain with shortness of breath
Severe sore throat with difficulty swallowing and no cough
Vomiting and diarrhea as the main symptoms without respiratory complaints
Symptoms that improve for a few days and then worsen with high fever (suggests secondary bacterial infection)

argues_against: Gradual onset over days with mild symptoms
Sudden pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea

negatives: Severe unilateral throat pain with drooling

argues_against: Vomiting and diarrhea as the only symptoms without respiratory complaints

general.mild: Alert, mildly ill-appearing, able to converse normally
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, flushed, prefers to lie still, voice may be hoarse
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, tachypneic, uncomfortable at rest
general.critical: Severely ill, lethargic or confused, labored breathing, signs of shock or respiratory failure

findings.finding: Fever, often 100.4–103°F

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient and ask about chills
findings.finding: Chills or shivering, sometimes rigors

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's general appearance and work of breathing
findings.finding: Ill-appearing, flushed, fatigued, prefers to lie still

findings.maneuver: Measure the heart rate and palpate the radial pulse
findings.finding: Tachycardia, often out of proportion to fever

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate over a full minute
findings.finding: Tachypnea

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx with a light and tongue blade
findings.finding: Diffuse pharyngeal erythema, sometimes with enlarged tonsils; no exudate
Erythematous, congested nasal mucosa with clear discharge
Conjunctival injection or watery eyes

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical lymph node chains
findings.finding: Tender, mildly enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient at rest and ask them to speak a full sentence
findings.finding: No respiratory distress or accessory muscle use

findings.maneuver: Assess neck stiffness and perform a brief neurologic screen
findings.finding: No neck stiffness, normal mental status, no focal deficits

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, including the trunk and extremities
findings.finding: No rash or petechiae

findings.maneuver: Inspect the tonsils and posterior pharynx
findings.finding: No tonsillar exudate or asymmetry

findings.maneuver: Palpate the neck for mass or asymmetry
findings.finding: No unilateral neck swelling or mass

labs.caveat: Often normal or mildly low from viral suppression; leukocytosis with a left shift suggests secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Relative lymphocytosis is common in viral illness; not specific for influenza.
Nonspecific; marked elevation should raise concern for bacterial superinfection.
Low values favor viral illness; higher values suggest bacterial coinfection.
Check when there is severe myalgia, dark urine, or weakness; elevation suggests influenza myositis or rhabdomyolysis.
Elevated only with severe illness, shock, or secondary bacterial sepsis.
Order when chest pain, dyspnea, or hemodynamic instability suggests myocarditis.
May rise with influenza-related myocarditis or heart failure exacerbation.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
Diffuse ST-segment elevation or depression suggesting myocarditis
T-wave inversions
New bundle branch block or AV block

findings.text: Patchy or lobar consolidation suggesting secondary bacterial pneumonia
Diffuse bilateral interstitial or alveolar opacities suggesting viral pneumonitis

imaging.preferred_when: Chest x-ray nondiagnostic but pneumonia or pneumonitis strongly suspected
Suspected myocarditis, pericarditis, or new heart failure

findings.text: Global or regional wall motion abnormality

initial.why: Rapid antigen or molecular test on a nasopharyngeal swab; confirms influenza and guides antiviral treatment
Assesses for leukocytosis suggesting bacterial superinfection or leukopenia from viral illness
initial.only_if: moderate to severe illness or concern for bacterial complication

initial.why: Assesses hydration and electrolytes in patients who are vomiting or dehydrated
Looks for pneumonia when hypoxia, abnormal lung exam, or persistent fever is present
initial.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (hypoxia, crackles, or worsening after initial improvement)

confirmatory.why: More sensitive than rapid antigen testing and distinguishes influenza A from B and other viruses
confirmatory.only_if: rapid test is negative but influenza is still suspected, or results will change management

supporting.why: Supports inflammation; marked elevation raises concern for bacterial coinfection
Low values favor viral illness and argue against bacterial pneumonia
Evaluates severe myalgia or dark urine for myositis or rhabdomyolysis
supporting.only_if: severe muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine

supporting.why: Evaluates for myocarditis when chest pain or dyspnea is present
supporting.only_if: chest pain, dyspnea, or hemodynamic instability

supporting.why: Assesses cardiac function and pericardial effusion when myocarditis is suspected
supporting.only_if: suspected myocarditis or new heart failure

not_indicated.why: Not routine in uncomplicated influenza with clear lungs and no hypoxia
Not needed unless complications are suspected and chest x-ray is nondiagnostic
No role in diagnosing influenza or its typical complications
Not indicated unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not indicated unless urinary symptoms or dehydration are present

decision_points: Antiviral treatment should start as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset, and should not be delayed while waiting for test results in high-risk or severely ill patients
A negative rapid influenza test does not rule out influenza when clinical suspicion is high; consider molecular testing
Consider bacterial superinfection if symptoms improve then worsen with fever, or if there is hypoxia, purulent sputum, or focal lung findings
Hospitalize for hypoxia, respiratory distress, altered mental status, inability to tolerate oral intake, or hemodynamic instability

differential.name: COVID-19
differential.why_considered: Overlapping febrile respiratory illness with cough, sore throat, myalgias, and fatigue, especially during respiratory virus season.
differential.trigger: Respiratory symptoms with fever during community circulation of SARS-CoV-2, or new loss of taste or smell.

history: Gradual or variable onset rather than the abrupt 'hit by a truck' onset of influenza
New loss of taste or smell
Known exposure to a person with COVID-19
exam: May have hypoxia with relatively mild lung findings
labs: Positive SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid amplification or antigen test
imaging: CT chest may show peripheral ground-glass opacities

differential.name: Bacterial pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Fever, cough, and malaise can mimic influenza, and bacterial pneumonia is a common complication of influenza.
differential.trigger: Focal lung findings, hypoxia, purulent sputum, or worsening after initial improvement.

history: Productive cough with purulent or blood-tinged sputum
Pleuritic chest pain
Symptoms that improve then worsen with recurrent fever
exam: Focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, dullness to percussion, or egophony
imaging: Lobar or segmental consolidation on chest x-ray

differential.name: Common cold (rhinovirus and other seasonal coronaviruses)
differential.why_considered: Nasal congestion, sore throat, and cough are shared with mild influenza.

history: Gradual onset over one to three days
Predominantly nasal congestion, sneezing, and sore throat
Fever is uncommon in adults
Mild fatigue without prominent body aches
exam: Nasal mucosal swelling with clear discharge
labs: Respiratory viral panel may identify rhinovirus or seasonal coronavirus

differential.name: Streptococcal pharyngitis
differential.why_considered: Sore throat and fever are prominent in both, and influenza can present with severe throat pain.

history: Sore throat is the dominant symptom
Cough and nasal congestion are typically absent
Abrupt onset of throat pain without prominent myalgias
exam: Tonsillar exudate, palatal petechiae, or tender anterior cervical adenopathy
Scarlet fever rash may be present
labs: Positive rapid antigen detection test or throat culture for group A Streptococcus

differential.name: Infectious mononucleosis
differential.why_considered: Fever, sore throat, fatigue, and malaise in adolescents and young adults.

history: Gradual onset over days to weeks
Severe sore throat with difficulty swallowing
Profound fatigue lasting weeks
labs: Positive heterophile antibody or EBV serology

differential.name: Acute bronchitis
differential.why_considered: Cough with chest discomfort and low-grade fever can resemble mild influenza.

history: Cough is the predominant symptom, often productive
Fever is low-grade or absent
Body aches and chills are minimal
exam: Diffuse wheezing or coarse breath sounds
imaging: Chest x-ray typically normal without consolidation

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Influenza can cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, especially in children, and patients may call this 'stomach flu.'

history: Vomiting and diarrhea are the primary symptoms
Respiratory complaints such as cough and sore throat are absent or minimal
Fever may be low-grade
exam: Diffuse abdominal tenderness without focal findings
Signs of dehydration may be present
labs: Stool testing may identify norovirus or other enteric pathogens

severity.mild: Afebrile or low-grade fever, mild cough and congestion, able to carry out usual activities with some difficulty, no risk factors for complications.
severity.moderate: Fever 100.4–102.2°F, prominent myalgias, headache, and cough, feels too unwell to work or attend school, but no respiratory distress or dehydration.
severity.severe: High fever, marked prostration, tachypnea, hypoxemia, or inability to tolerate oral intake; may require hospitalization, especially with underlying chronic disease.
severity.critical: Respiratory failure, shock, encephalopathy, or myocarditis requiring intensive care; most often in older adults, infants, pregnant people, or the immunocompromised.

red_flags.finding: Shortness of breath at rest or oxygen saturation below 92%
red_flags.meaning: Suggests viral pneumonitis or secondary bacterial pneumonia; needs urgent evaluation and imaging.

red_flags.finding: Symptoms improve for a few days then worsen with high fever and productive cough
red_flags.meaning: Classic pattern of secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Possible influenza encephalopathy, sepsis, or severe dehydration; requires emergent workup.
Raises concern for myocarditis or pericarditis.

red_flags.finding: Severe muscle pain with dark urine or weakness
Inability to keep fluids down or signs of dehydration
red_flags.meaning: May require intravenous fluids and hospitalization.

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or tachycardia out of proportion to fever

complications.name: Secondary bacterial pneumonia
clues: Improvement followed by worsening fever and cough
Focal crackles or consolidation on chest x-ray

complications.name: Primary influenza viral pneumonia
clues: Rapid progression of dyspnea and hypoxemia within 1–2 days of onset
Diffuse bilateral opacities on chest imaging

complications.name: Myocarditis or pericarditis
clues: New ECG changes or elevated troponin

complications.name: Encephalitis or encephalopathy
clues: Altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits

complications.name: Sinusitis
clues: Persistent nasal congestion and purulent discharge

complications.name: Exacerbation of chronic disease (asthma, COPD, heart failure, diabetes)

special_populations.differences: Vomiting and diarrhea are more common; febrile seizures can occur; otitis media and croup are more frequent complications. Children under 5, especially under 2, are at higher risk of severe disease.
May present with fever, poor feeding, lethargy, or apnea rather than classic cough and myalgias; sepsis evaluation is often considered.
May lack fever and present with weakness, confusion, or decompensation of chronic illness; higher risk of pneumonia, hospitalization, and death.
Higher risk of severe illness, hospitalization, preterm labor, and fetal complications; antiviral treatment should be started promptly and is recommended in pregnancy.
Prolonged viral shedding, atypical or more severe presentation, higher risk of viral pneumonia and bacterial superinfection; may require extended antiviral therapy.
Higher risk of severe influenza and of hyperglycemia or diabetic ketoacidosis during illness; monitor glucose closely.
Higher risk of severe influenza, hospitalization, and respiratory failure.

key_questions.question: How did your symptoms start — suddenly or gradually?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset over a few hours; patients often can name the hour they started feeling sick

key_questions.question: When did the symptoms start?
key_questions.looking_for: Within the last 1–2 days; determines whether antiviral therapy can still be started within 48 hours

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or feeling feverish with chills or shivering; not everyone with influenza has a fever

key_questions.question: Do your muscles or body ache?
key_questions.looking_for: Prominent diffuse myalgias, often described as feeling like being hit by a truck

key_questions.question: How severe is your fatigue?
key_questions.looking_for: Marked prostration and weakness, worse than a typical cold

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough, sore throat, or runny nose?
key_questions.looking_for: Dry or minimally productive cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion accompanying the systemic symptoms

key_questions.question: Have you had any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Sometimes present, more common in children; vomiting and diarrhea as the only symptoms suggest gastroenteritis rather than influenza

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you been sick with fever, cough, and body aches?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts at home, school, or work, or influenza circulating in the community during flu season

key_questions.question: Have you been vaccinated against influenza this season?
key_questions.looking_for: Not vaccinated increases likelihood; vaccination reduces risk and severity but does not rule out influenza

key_questions.question: Do you have any chronic conditions such as asthma, diabetes, heart disease, or kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that increase the risk of complications and lower the threshold for antiviral treatment

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant, or could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy increases the risk of severe illness; antiviral treatment is recommended and should be started promptly

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medications that weaken your immune system, such as steroids or chemotherapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression, which raises the risk of severe or prolonged illness

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath at rest, or does it hurt to breathe?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea or pleuritic chest pain suggesting pneumonia, viral pneumonitis, or myocarditis

key_questions.question: Did your symptoms improve and then get worse again with a new fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Classic pattern of secondary bacterial pneumonia

key_questions.question: Have you been confused, unusually sleepy, or unable to keep fluids down?
key_questions.looking_for: Encephalopathy, severe dehydration, or sepsis requiring urgent evaluation

reasoning_points: Abrupt onset of fever, chills, myalgias, and fatigue over a few hours
Prominent systemic symptoms with dry cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion
Sick contact or community circulation of influenza during fall or winter
Absence of gradual-onset, predominantly nasal symptoms typical of a common cold
No focal lung findings, hypoxia, or purulent sputum to suggest bacterial pneumonia
Rapid influenza test or molecular testing confirms influenza when obtained
Risk factors for complications (age, pregnancy, chronic disease, immunosuppression) identified to guide antiviral treatment

easy: Classic abrupt onset of fever, chills, myalgias, and cough during flu season
Clear sick contact at home, school, or work
Ill-appearing but lungs clear and no hypoxia
medium: Older adult without fever presenting with weakness or confusion
Patient with asthma or COPD whose respiratory symptoms are worsening
Symptoms overlap with COVID-19 or another respiratory virus
Negative rapid antigen test but high clinical suspicion
hard: Infant with fever, poor feeding, and lethargy rather than classic cough and myalgias
Pregnant patient with severe illness and concern for complications
Immunocompromised patient with prolonged or atypical presentation
Symptoms improve then worsen with high fever and productive cough suggesting secondary bacterial pneumonia
Chest pain or dyspnea raising concern for myocarditis
